title: Subarray with Given Sum
problem: Given an unsorted array `arr` of size `N` containing non-negative integers, find a continuous sub-array that adds up to a given number `S`. In case of multiple subarrays, return the 1-based indices of the first occurrence from the left.

examples.explanation: The sum of elements from 2nd position to 4th position is 2 + 3 + 7 = 12.

approach: Maintain a variable-sized sliding window defined by `[left, right]`. Accumulate `current_sum += arr[right]`. While `current_sum > S` and `left < right`, subtract `arr[left]` and advance `left`. If `current_sum == S`, return `{left + 1, right + 1}` (1-based index).

complexity.time: O(N) — each element is added and removed at most once

title: Missing Number in Array
problem: Given an array of size `N-1` such that it only contains distinct integers in the range of `1` to `N`. Find the missing element.
approach: We can use XOR bitwise manipulation to avoid integer overflow issues with large N. Compute `XOR_all = 1 ^ 2 ^ ... ^ N` and `XOR_arr = A[0] ^ A[1] ^ ... ^ A[N-2]`. The missing number is `XOR_all ^ XOR_arr` because identical numbers cancel out to 0 (`x ^ x = 0`).

complexity.time: O(N) — single pass to XOR numbers

title: Detect Loop in Linked List
topic: Linked List · Two Pointers · Floyd's Cycle Finding
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine if the linked list has a loop. A loop exists if a node can be reached again by continuously traversing following the `next` pointer.
approach: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm. Initialize two pointers, `slow` and `fast`, at the head. Advance `slow` by 1 step and `fast` by 2 steps. If there is a loop, `fast` will eventually lap and meet `slow`. If `fast` reaches `null`, the list is linear.

complexity.time: O(N) — fast pointer catches slow within cycle length

title: Kth Smallest Element
problem: Given an array `arr[]` of `N` distinct integers and a number `K`, where `K` is smaller than the size of the array. Find the `K-th` smallest element in the given array.
approach: Maintain a Max-Heap of size `K`. Push elements into the heap. Whenever the heap size exceeds `K`, pop the root (the maximum among them). After inspecting all `N` elements, the top of the max-heap will be the `K-th` smallest element.

complexity.time: O(N log K) — maintaining a heap of size K
complexity.space: O(K) — for storing K elements in heap

title: Parenthesis Checker
problem: Given an expression string `x`. Examine whether the pairs and the orders of `{`, `}`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]` are correct in exp.
approach: Traverse each character. If it is an opening delimiter, push it to stack. If it is a closing delimiter, check if stack is empty or if popped opening delimiter does not match. At end, stack must be empty.

title: Next Greater Element
problem: Given an array `arr[ ]` of size `N` having elements, the task is to find the next greater element for each element of the array in order of their appearance in the array. If no next greater element exists, output `-1`.
approach: Traverse array from right to left while maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack. For current element `arr[i]`, pop all elements from stack that are `<= arr[i]`. If stack is non-empty, top is next greater element; otherwise `-1`. Push current element onto stack.

complexity.time: O(N) — each element pushed and popped at most once
complexity.space: O(N) — stack stores up to N elements

title: Check for BST
topic: Tree · Binary Search Tree · Inorder Traversal
problem: Given the root of a binary tree. Check whether it is a BST or not. Note: We consider that either keys in left subtree are smaller than root key and keys in right subtree are greater than root key.
approach: An Inorder Traversal of a valid Binary Search Tree always produces a strictly sorted ascending sequence. We can perform an inorder traversal while keeping track of `prev_val`. If current node's value is `<= prev_val`, the tree is not a BST.

complexity.space: O(H) — call stack bounded by tree height

title: Rat in a Maze Problem
problem: Consider a rat placed at `(0, 0)` in a square matrix `m` of order `n*n`. It has to reach destination `(n-1, n-1)`. Find all possible paths that the rat can take to reach from source to destination. Directions are 'U'(up), 'D'(down), 'L'(left), 'R'(right). `0` means blocked and `1` means open.
approach: Backtracking DFS with 4 directional steps in lexicographical order: `D` (down), `L` (left), `R` (right), `U` (up). Mark the current cell visited (e.g. `m[r][c] = 0`), recurse, then unmark upon return (`m[r][c] = 1`).

complexity.time: O(4^(N^2)) — worst-case exploration of all maze paths
complexity.space: O(N * N) — recursion depth bounded by total cells

title: Minimum Number of Jumps
problem: Given an array `arr[]` of size `n` of non-negative integers. Each array element represents the maximum length of the jumps that can be made forward from that element. Find the minimum number of jumps to reach the end of the array from start (index 0). If an element is 0, they cannot move through that element. Return -1 if impossible.
approach: Greedy BFS interval approach. Track `maxReach` (farthest reachable index), `steps` remaining in current jump range, and `jumps` count. When `i` reaches current jump boundary, increment `jumps` and update range.

complexity.time: O(N) — single forward pass through array

title: Longest Common Subsequence
problem: Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, find the length of the longest subsequence present in both of them. A subsequence is a sequence that appears in the same relative order, but not necessarily contiguous.
approach: 2D Dynamic Programming. Let `dp[i][j]` be the length of LCS of `s1[0..i-1]` and `s2[0..j-1]`. If `s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]`, then `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]`. Otherwise, `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.

complexity.time: O(N * M) — nested loop through grid
complexity.space: O(N * M) — DP table size (can be optimized to O(M))
